name: Sauvage / Bleu de Chanel compliment getters
lead: "Compliment getter" is fragrance-community slang for a scent said to draw positive comments from other people. Dior Sauvage and Bleu de Chanel are two best-selling men's fragrances frequently named in this context, and people wear them as part of grooming: a pleasant, recognisable scent is treated as part of how attractive and put-together someone seems in close contact.

Bleu de Chanel was released by the French house Chanel in 2010 as a woody aromatic fragrance created by perfumer Jacques Polge.[1] It won the 2011 FiFi Award for Best New Male Fragrance, and ranked among the best-selling men's fragrances in the US in 2011 and 2012.[1] Dior's Sauvage name echoes the earlier Eau Sauvage, Dior's first men's fragrance, released in 1966 with perfumer Edmond Roudnitska.[3]
No published study located has tested whether either fragrance elicits more compliments or improves perceived attractiveness.
infobox: 2011 FiFi Award, Best New Male Fragrance
Parfum 15-30%, eau de parfum 15-20%, eau de toilette 5-15% (typical ranges)[2]

paras: Top notes include lemon, mint, pink pepper and grapefruit; heart notes include ginger, nutmeg, jasmine and Iso E Super; base notes include labdanum, sandalwood, patchouli, vetiver, incense, cedar and white musk.[1] Martin Scorsese directed the launch commercial, with actor Gaspard Ulliel as the first face of the fragrance from 2010 until his death in 2022.[1] Timothée Chalamet became ambassador in 2023.[1]
It was a top Christmas seller at Bloomingdale's in 2010 and the second most popular fragrance in Britain in 2021.[1]

Dior's Eau Sauvage was released in 1966 as the house's first men's fragrance, composed by Edmond Roudnitska, with top notes of lemon, bergamot, basil, rosemary and caraway; actor Alain Delon appeared in its launch advertising, and the name came from Christian Dior's friend Percy Savage, whom he was introduced to as "Monsieur Sauvage".[3] The modern Dior Sauvage line is a separate product; details on it were not available from the sources reviewed.

Fragrances marketed to men have historically been sold mostly as eau de toilette or cologne, with more eau de parfum and extrait versions appearing as scents become more unisex.[2] Higher concentration generally means stronger scent and longer duration, with rough figures of 2 to 4 hours for eau de toilette and up to 6 to 8 for perfume; dry skin holds scent for less time than oilier skin.[2]

Fragrance communities discuss popular designer scents as "safe" or crowd-pleasing options and trade reports of compliments. These accounts are anecdotal; specific community sources were not available for citation.
No studies found. Broader research on fragrance and perceived attractiveness was not reviewed for this article.

card.summary: Two hugely popular men's designer scents that fragrance communities call crowd-pleasers; the compliment claims are anecdotal.
card.note: No studies test compliment rates; Sauvage coverage in sources is limited.

quick.overview:
Sauvage and Bleu de Chanel are among the best-selling men's fragrances and are often called "compliment getters" in fragrance communities.

Sales and awards are documented for Bleu de Chanel; claims about compliments are personal reports and have not been studied.
quick.mechanism: People wear a popular, widely liked scent and report on reactions from others.
quick.risks: Fragrance can cause skin allergy or breathing irritation in some people; otherwise main cost is price.

chain: Wear a widely liked designer fragrance
Pleasant scent noticed at close range
Positive comments and a more polished impression
angle.text: Wearers choose these scents because fragrance communities report them as broadly liked and often complimented. The benefit is reported anecdotally and has not been measured.
